entries.clause: adverbial clause of time (the same word is also a preposition and an adverb)
entries.pattern: After [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] after [clause]. · [main clause] [measure phrase] after [clause] (ten minutes after everyone left). · Just / right / soon / shortly / long after [clause], [main clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the after clause when it comes first; no comma when it follows.
entries.meaning: Marks the main clause event as following the after clause event. With a clause it is a conjunction (after the show ended); with a noun phrase or an -ing form (after the show, after eating) the same word is a preposition; standing alone behind a measure phrase it is an adverb (she called two days after). Do not put will inside the clause: after I get home, never after I will get home.
examples: After the movie ended, we walked to the diner.
She called me after she landed in Denver.
After you finish the dishes, could you take the trash out?
The alarm went off ten minutes after everyone had already left.
After the storm passed, the whole street smelled like wet pine.
Just after I hit send, I noticed the typo.

entries.clause: adverbial clause of time (the same word also builds clauses of cause, manner, comparison, and concession, and works as a preposition)
entries.pattern: As [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] as [clause]. · Just as [clause], [main clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the as clause when it comes first; usually no comma when it follows. The comma does not disambiguate the time reading from the cause reading, so rewrite with while or because if a sentence could go either way.
entries.meaning: Sets two events side by side in time, usually with a sense that they unfold together rather than meeting at a single point. When names a moment and while spans a stretch; as is the one that runs two things in parallel, which makes it the natural choice for gradual change (as the days got shorter). It is the most overloaded word in this file: besides time it gives a reason (as it was late, we left), a manner (do as I do), a comparison (as tall as his brother), and a grudging concession (tired as he was, he finished), and with a noun phrase it is a preposition instead (as a child, works as a nurse). That crowding is exactly why as is a bad choice whenever a reader might hear 'because.'
examples: As the bell rang, half the class was already standing.
She hummed as she worked.
As the years went by, the letters came less often.
Just as I sat down, the phone rang.
The crowd got quieter as the speaker went on.
As we drove west, the mountains came into view.

entries.clause: adverbial clause of time (the same word is also a preposition and an adverb)
entries.pattern: Before [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] before [clause]. · It was [measure phrase] before [clause] (a good ten minutes before anybody spoke). · Just / right / shortly / long before [clause], [main clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the before clause when it comes first; no comma when it follows.
entries.meaning: The exact mirror of after: the main clause event precedes the before clause event. Keep the clause in the present when the reference is future (before she gets here). Only the clause use is the conjunction - with a noun phrase it is a preposition (before noon), and on its own it is an adverb (I've seen this before). Note the idiomatic 'and it never happened' reading in sentences like He hung up before I could thank him, where the before event is exactly the one that did not occur.
examples: Before you leave, make sure the back door is locked.
We got the tent up before it started raining.
He hung up before I could explain.
Before the bridge was built, the trip took two hours.
Call me before you buy anything.
It was a good ten minutes before anybody said a word.

entries.clause: adverbial clause of time (the same word is separately an adverb, and that is its commoner job - I met him once, the once-great franchise)
entries.pattern: Once [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] once [clause]. · Once [past participle or adjective phrase], [main clause] (reduced clause: once installed, once cool enough to handle).
entries.punctuation: Comma after the once clause when it comes first; usually no comma when it follows.
variants: none as a conjunction - once is separately an adverb meaning 'one time' and 'formerly' (I met him once, the once-great franchise)
entries.meaning: Means 'from the moment that,' with the added sense that the event is a threshold: once the paperwork clears implies everything else was waiting on it. When is neutral about that dependency and as soon as stresses speed; once stresses that the condition, having been met, stays met. It also reduces cleanly in instructions (once installed, once cool enough to handle), where the subject and be drop out. The word is an adverb far more often than it is a conjunction, and the clause test sorts them: I met him once has nothing following, so there is no conjunction there.
examples: Once the paperwork clears, the money moves the same day.
You'll like him once you get to know him.
Once she made up her mind, there was no talking her out of it.
The engine runs fine once it warms up.
Once we crossed the state line, the radio stations all changed.
It gets easier once you stop overthinking it.
Once cool enough to handle, the pan goes in the top rack. (reduced clause)

entries.clause: adverbial clause of time (the same word also builds clauses of cause, and works as a preposition and an adverb)
entries.pattern: Since [clause], [main clause with a perfect tense]. · [main clause with a perfect tense] since [clause]. · Ever since [clause], [main clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the since clause when it comes first; no comma when it follows.
entries.meaning: Marks the start of a stretch that runs up to now, which is why the main clause almost always takes a perfect tense: I've lived here since I was ten, not I live here since I was ten. The clause itself normally takes the simple past. It is a conjunction only in front of a clause: with a noun phrase it is a preposition (since Tuesday) and standing alone it is an adverb (I haven't seen her since). The collision with the cause reading is real - Since you took over, things have gone smoothly genuinely has two meanings, and ever since or because is the fix.
examples: She's been quieter since her sister moved out.
Since the new manager started, the schedule has actually made sense.
I haven't touched a cigarette since I got out of the hospital.
Ever since we got the dog, nobody sleeps past six.
Since they repaved the road, the drive has taken fifteen minutes less.
He's called twice since you left.

entries.clause: adverbial clause of time (the same word is also a preposition: till Friday, till noon)
entries.pattern: Till [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] till [clause]. · [negative main clause] till [clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the till clause when it comes first, which is uncommon; no comma when it follows.
entries.meaning: Means exactly what until means, and takes a clause or a noun phrase for the same reason until does - conjunction in front of a clause, preposition in front of a noun. Despite appearances till is the older word and not a clipping of until, which is why the apostrophe in 'til is a back-formation that editors delete. Use until at the start of a sentence and in formal writing; till is at home in speech and casual prose.
examples: Stir it till the sugar dissolves.
We stayed till the last band finished.
I didn't know he was sick till somebody told me at work.
Just hold the door till I get the stroller through.
Nobody moved till the coach blew the whistle.
Till I saw the bill, I had no idea how much we'd spent.
She kept refreshing the page till the grades posted.

entries.clause: adverbial clause of time (the same word is also a preposition: until noon)
entries.pattern: Until [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] until [clause]. · [negative main clause] until [clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the until clause when it comes first; no comma when it follows.
entries.meaning: Marks the endpoint of a situation that continues up to it. In front of a clause it is a conjunction; in front of a noun phrase (until Friday) the same word is a preposition. Keep the clause in the present for future reference (until she gets back). The most useful pattern is the negative one: not ... until is how English says 'only at that point' - The store doesn't open until ten is a statement about ten o'clock, not about the store being closed forever.
examples: Wait here until I call you.
Until the results came back, nobody said anything out loud.
The store doesn't open until ten.
We kept the heat on until the pipes thawed.
He didn't tell his parents until the semester was over.
Until you've tried it yourself, don't knock it.

entries.ipa: /wɛn/, weak /wən/; some Southern and older speakers keep /ʍɛn/
entries.clause: adverbial clause of time (the same word also introduces noun clauses and relative clauses - I know when he left, the year when we moved - and is the interrogative adverb in questions: When did you leave?)
entries.pattern: When [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] when [clause]. · when + [-ing form or past participle] (reduced clause: when finished, when driving).
entries.punctuation: Comma after the when clause when it comes first; no comma when it follows. Use a comma before a trailing when clause only when it is an afterthought or a surprise turn, and note that the comma is the only thing marking that reading: She was halfway through the story when her phone rang (plain time) versus She was halfway through the story, when the lights went out (the interruption).
entries.meaning: The default time subordinator: it puts the main clause at the point named by the when clause. While spreads the event across a stretch, as runs the two together, and when simply says 'at that time.' Never use will inside it - when he gets here, not when he will get here.
examples: When the power went out, the whole block came outside.
Call me when you get in.
When I was a kid, we drove to Michigan every August.
She was halfway through the story when her phone rang.
When the check finally cleared, I felt like I could breathe.
Text me when you're five minutes out.

entries.clause: adverbial clause of time (also concessive, 'no matter when')
entries.pattern: Whenever [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] whenever [clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the whenever clause when it comes first; no comma when it follows.
variants: when ever as two words only in questions (When ever did you find the time?)
entries.meaning: Means 'every time that' or 'at whatever time,' where when means 'at that one time.' The frequency reading is the common one: whenever it rains covers all the rainy days, while when it rained points at one. The second reading - 'it doesn't matter when' - shows up in offers and permissions.
examples: Whenever it rains, that corner floods.
She calls her mother whenever she has a long drive.
Whenever you're ready, we'll start.
The dog hides whenever the vacuum comes out.
Whenever I try to cook rice, it turns to glue.
Stop by whenever you want - we're home all weekend.

entries.clause: adverbial clause of time (the same word also builds clauses of contrast and of concession, and is separately a noun and a verb)
entries.pattern: While [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] while [clause]. · while + [-ing form, past participle, adjective phrase, or prepositional phrase] (reduced clause).
entries.punctuation: Comma after the while clause when it comes first. When it follows, no comma in the time sense - but do use a comma when while means 'whereas,' because that reading is contrastive and non-restrictive: She read while I cooked (time) versus She loves horror movies, while I can't watch them (contrast).
entries.meaning: Spans a stretch of time and puts the main clause inside it. When names a point and as runs two events together; while is the one that means 'throughout.' The reduced form (while waiting, while in college) is extremely common in edited prose, and the contrast sense is common enough that the comma rule above is worth memorizing. Beyond the conjunction, while is a noun (stay a while, worth your while) and a verb (while away an afternoon), so the clause test decides the reading here too.
examples: While the sauce simmers, chop the parsley.
She read while I cooked.
Somebody took my seat while I was in the restroom.
While I was living in Tucson, I never once used the heater.
He learned Portuguese while working on a rig off Brazil.
While we waited for the tow truck, three people stopped to ask if we were okay.

entries.ipa: /ˈæftər wɪtʃ/; which is /ʍɪtʃ/ for speakers who keep the wh
entries.respell: AF-ter-WICH; HWICH for speakers who keep the wh
entries.clause: adverbial relative clause of time, always non-restrictive; the relative which points back at the whole preceding clause rather than at any single noun
entries.pattern: [main clause], after which [clause]. · [long main clause]; after which [clause]. · [main clause], after which [clause], [continuation]. · There is no fronted skeleton - After which [clause], [main clause] is not a sentence.
entries.punctuation: Always preceded by a comma, or by a semicolon in a long sentence; never followed by one. Like whereupon, its clause cannot move to the front, so after which can never open a sentence in edited prose - a stray After which... is a fragment, whatever effect the writer was after.
entries.meaning: The plain modern way to keep a narrative moving without starting a new sentence: which reaches back over everything just said, and after puts the next event behind it. Whereupon says nearly the same thing but adds a hint that the first event triggered the second, and it carries a distinctly literary tone; after which is neutral about cause and is at home in minutes, reports, procedures, and news writing. Because the relative looks backward, the clause is stuck at the end of its sentence.
examples: The committee heard forty minutes of testimony, after which the chair called for a vote.
She finished her residency in Cleveland, after which she moved to Santa Fe and opened a practice.
The system runs a full backup at two in the morning, after which the nightly reports are generated.
He was suspended for three games, after which he was quietly traded.
Guests check in at the front desk, after which a shuttle takes them out to the cabins.
The tenant has thirty days to cure the default, after which the landlord may terminate the lease.

entries.clause: adverbial clause of time
entries.pattern: Any time [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] any time [clause]. · Any time that [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] any time that [clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the any time clause when it comes first; no comma when it follows. The optional that is usually dropped.
entries.meaning: A near-synonym of whenever with a permissive edge: any time you need help offers all the occasions, where every time merely counts them. Write it as one word in the conjunction and adverb uses (anytime you want); keep two words after a preposition and when any modifies a real quantity (at any time, do you have any time?).
examples: Anytime you need a ride, just text me.
She gets a headache any time the pressure drops.
Anytime somebody mentions the merger, he changes the subject.
Call the front desk any time the heat cuts out.
Anytime I've asked him for a favor, he's said yes.
You can return it any time the store is open.

entries.clause: adverbial clause of time (the same phrase also builds clauses of condition)
entries.pattern: As long as [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] as long as [clause]. · [main clause] for as long as [clause]. · So long as [clause], [main clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the as long as clause when it comes first; no comma when it follows.
entries.meaning: In the time sense it means 'throughout the whole period that': the main clause holds for exactly the stretch the clause describes. In the conditional sense it means 'provided that.' Context decides - as long as the music played is duration, as long as you pay on time is a condition. The comparison as long as ('of equal length') is a third construction entirely.
examples: The porch light stays on as long as somebody's still out.
As long as the generator held out, we had lights.
She'll keep coaching as long as the kids keep showing up.
So long as you're standing there, hand me the pliers.
I'll stay as long as you need me.
As long as the ice held, the whole town skated on it.

entries.ipa: /æz ˈɔfən æz/, reduced /əz ˈɔfən əz/; many speakers have /ˈɑfən/ with the cot-caught merger, and the t is silent for nearly all of them - the spelling pronunciation /ˈɔftən/ is a minority form and not the default
entries.clause: adverbial clause of time (frequency)
entries.pattern: As often as [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] as often as [clause]. · [main clause] as often as [noun phrase] (comparison - a different construction).
entries.punctuation: Comma after the as often as clause when it comes first; no comma when it follows.
entries.meaning: The frequency member of the family: it counts the occasions the way every time does, but folds in a note of concession - as often as I've told him means 'on all those occasions, and there have been plenty of them.' Keep it apart from the comparative as often as, which measures one frequency against another (She calls as often as I do) and is not a time clause at all.
examples: As often as I've driven that road, I still miss the turn.
He brings it up as often as he can work it into a conversation.
As often as that machine jams, somebody ought to replace it.
She gets out to see her grandmother as often as the weather lets her.
As often as we've been through this, you'd think I'd remember the password.
The alarm goes off as often as a truck backs into the loading dock.

entries.ipa: /æz ˈsun æz/, reduced /əz ˈsun əz/, often collapsing to /əˈsunəz/
entries.clause: adverbial clause of time
entries.pattern: As soon as [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] as soon as [clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the as soon as clause when it comes first; no comma when it follows.
variants: soon as (the clipped spoken American form: soon as I get there, I'll call)
entries.meaning: Says the main clause happens immediately after the clause event, with no gap in between. When allows a delay, once stresses that a threshold has been crossed, and as soon as stresses speed. Use the present for future reference - as soon as I land, never as soon as I will land.
examples: I'll call you as soon as I land.
As soon as the light turned green, the guy behind me leaned on the horn.
She recognized the voice as soon as he said hello.
As soon as we're done here, I'm going home.
Text me as soon as you hear anything.
As soon as the check cleared, he booked the flight.

entries.ipa: /æt sʌtʃ ˈtaɪm əz/; at reduces to /ət/ and the final as rarely carries stress
entries.clause: adverbial clause of time
entries.pattern: At such time as [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] at such time as [clause]. · [subject] shall [verb] at such time as [clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the at such time as clause when it comes first; no comma when it follows.
variants: until such time as (the endpoint version)
at such time or times as (drafting boilerplate)
at such time that (a common miswriting)
entries.meaning: When, dressed for a contract. The phrase names a future point whose date nobody yet knows, which is exactly why drafters reach for it: at such time as the board determines leaves the timing open in a way on July 1 cannot. It is the point-in-time partner of [until such time as](#until-such-time-as), and an American meets it in stock plans, trust instruments, court orders, and personnel manuals and almost nowhere else. Outside those registers it is padding, and editors cut it back to when.
examples: The remaining shares vest at such time as the company completes an initial public offering.
At such time as the tenant assigns the lease, the guaranty terminates automatically.
Distributions shall be made at such time as the trustee in her sole discretion determines.
The department will reopen the position at such time as funding is restored.
At such time as the court enters final judgment, the escrowed funds shall be released.
Plain English: The remaining shares vest when the company goes public.

entries.clause: adverbial relative clause of time, always non-restrictive; which points back at the whole preceding clause or at a date named in it
entries.pattern: [main clause], at which time [clause]. · [long main clause]; at which time [clause]. · [main clause], at which point [clause] (the everyday variant). · No fronted skeleton - the clause cannot open a sentence.
entries.punctuation: Always preceded by a comma, or by a semicolon in a long sentence; never followed by one. It can never start a sentence, and the comma in front of it is not optional, because the clause is non-restrictive.
variants: at which point (commoner in ordinary prose)
when (after a named date: on June 1, when...)
entries.meaning: The plain-prose replacement for whereupon: it drops the second event onto exactly the moment the first one reached. At which point is the same connector with less starch and is what most Americans actually say; at which time is the one that turns up in agendas, contracts, and meeting minutes. Keep it apart from its two neighbors in the family - after which only says 'later than that,' and by which time says the second event was already finished.
examples: The public comment period closes on March 3, at which time the board will take up the ordinance.
We waited until the last flight was called, at which time the agent finally admitted the crew was stuck in Denver.
The note matures in five years, at which time the full principal comes due.
Training runs through Friday, at which time new hires are assigned to a shift.
The alarm sounded twice, at which point everybody stopped pretending it was a drill.
The deposition was suspended at 4:15 p.m., at which time counsel conferred off the record.

entries.clause: adverbial clause of time
entries.pattern: By the time [clause], [main clause with had + past participle]. · By the time [clause], [main clause with will have + past participle]. · [main clause] by the time [clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the by the time clause when it comes first; no comma when it follows.
entries.meaning: Means 'at or before the moment when,' and it pulls a perfect tense into the main clause: past perfect for past reference (by the time we got there, they had left) and future perfect for future reference (by the time you read this, I'll have landed). When just marks the point; by the time says the main clause was already complete at that point.
examples: By the time we got there, they had already left.
By the time you read this, I'll have landed in Seattle.
The soup was cold by the time everyone sat down.
By the time she turned thirty, she'd lived in six cities.
By the time the inspector showed up, we'd fixed it ourselves.
He'll be asleep by the time the game ends.

entries.clause: adverbial relative clause of time, always non-restrictive; which points back at a moment already named
entries.pattern: [main clause], by which time [clause with a perfect tense]. · [long main clause]; by which time [clause]. · [main clause], by which point [clause]. · No fronted skeleton - the clause cannot open a sentence.
entries.punctuation: Always preceded by a comma, or by a semicolon in a long sentence; never followed by one. It can never start a sentence.
variants: by then (the adverb equivalent, which needs no preceding clause)
entries.meaning: [By the time](#by-the-time) turned around. Instead of naming the deadline in a clause of its own, it points back at a moment already on the page, and it drags the same perfect tense along with it: by which time everyone had left. It nearly always carries a note of too late. Set it against its neighbors: at which time puts the second event right at that moment, while by which time says the second event was over before the moment arrived.
examples: The tow truck showed up at eleven, by which time we had already changed the tire ourselves.
Her flight was rerouted through Charlotte, by which time the connection had long since departed.
The report reached the committee in June, by which time two of its authors had left the agency.
He apologized the following spring, by which time nobody could remember what the fight had been about.
Repairs are scheduled for next October, by which time the building will have stood empty for three years.
The recall notice finally went out in the middle of March, by which point most of the affected units had already been installed in new houses.

entries.ipa: /ˈdʊrɪŋ ðə ˈtaɪm ðət/; also /ˈdjʊrɪŋ/ for older and Southern speakers
entries.clause: adverbial clause of time (duration)
entries.pattern: During the time that [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] during the time that [clause]. · During the period that / during the time when [clause], [main clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the during the time that clause when it comes first; no comma when it follows. Unlike most of the optional thats in this file, this one does not drop comfortably: during the time he was in office is possible but reads as a slip.
entries.meaning: A four-word while, kept alive by contracts, testimony, and academic prose, where a writer wants the stretch stated as a stretch. It differs from while in weight and in one honest particular: while has a contrast sense (she likes it, while I don't) that this phrase cannot have, so it is unambiguous where while is not. That is the only real argument for it. In ordinary writing, cut it to while.
examples: During the time that he served as treasurer, the fund never missed a filing deadline.
No interest accrues during the time that the account is under review.
During the time that the plant sat idle, the company continued to pay full benefits.
She was living in Seattle during the time that the bridge was being rebuilt.
During the time that the witness was in the room, did anyone speak to her about the report?
Plain English: While he was treasurer, the fund never missed a filing deadline.

entries.clause: adverbial relative clause of time (duration), always non-restrictive; which points back at a stretch already named
entries.pattern: [main clause naming a stretch], during which time [clause]. · [main clause], during which [clause] (the short form). · [long main clause]; during which time [clause]. · No fronted skeleton - the clause cannot open a sentence.
entries.punctuation: Always preceded by a comma, or by a semicolon in a long sentence; never followed by one. It can never start a sentence, and because the clause is non-restrictive the comma in front of it is required, not optional.
variants: during which (the bare form, when the antecedent is already a time noun)
entries.meaning: The duration member of the connective-relative family. After which and at which time point at a moment; this one covers a span, and it needs a span in front of it to point back at - for eleven days, during which time the detour added forty minutes works because eleven days is sitting there to be picked up. Drop the word time when the antecedent is already a time noun and the reference is obvious; keep it when a bare which would otherwise reach for the nearest ordinary noun instead.
examples: The road was closed for eleven days, during which time the detour added forty minutes to every commute.
He spent two years in Manila, during which time he learned enough Tagalog to argue with a landlord.
The system was offline from midnight to six, during which time no transactions were recorded.
She sat through a four-hour hearing, during which not one member asked her a question.
The lease ran through 2019, during which time the rent was never once raised.
There was a long silence, during which everybody at the table studied the tablecloth.

entries.clause: adverbial clause of time
entries.pattern: Each time [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] each time [clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the each time clause when it comes first; no comma when it follows.
entries.meaning: Means 'on every one of the occasions when,' and it differs from every time the way each differs from every everywhere else in the language: each takes the occasions one at a time, every takes them as a set. The difference is small enough that the two are usually interchangeable; each time sounds slightly more deliberate.
examples: Each time the door opened, everyone looked up.
She writes down the mileage each time she fills the tank.
Each time I've called, I've gotten a different answer.
The machine resets each time it loses power.
Each time he told the story, the fish got bigger.
They pat him down each time he comes through security.

entries.clause: adverbial clause of time
entries.pattern: Every time [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] every time [clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the every time clause when it comes first; no comma when it follows.
entries.meaning: The most common way to say 'on all the occasions when.' It overlaps almost completely with whenever, but every time counts the occasions and often carries a note of exasperation, where whenever is neutral and can also mean 'at whatever time suits you.'
examples: Every time I wash the car, it rains.
The floor creaks every time somebody walks past the bathroom.
Every time we try to leave, somebody starts a new conversation.
She wins every time we play.
Every single time I've flown through Atlanta, I've been delayed.
He apologizes every time he's late, and then he's late again.

entries.ipa: /ˌɛvər ˈsɪns/, run together in casual speech as /ˈɛvərsɪns/
entries.clause: adverbial clause of time (the same two words are also a bare adverb - He hasn't called ever since - and a preposition in front of a noun phrase: ever since college)
entries.pattern: Ever since [clause], [main clause with a perfect tense]. · [main clause with a perfect tense] ever since [clause]. · [main clause] ever since (bare adverb - nothing follows). · Ever since [noun phrase], [main clause] (preposition, not conjunction).
entries.punctuation: Comma after the ever since clause when it comes first; no comma when it follows. Nothing changes when it is the bare adverb at the end of a sentence: no comma there either.
variants: ever since then (pointing back at a moment already named)
since (the bare form, which leaves the 'because' reading open)
entries.meaning: Since with the ambiguity welded shut. The ever is not decoration - it blocks the causal reading outright, so ever since you took over can only be about time, where since you took over can be read either way. In every other respect it behaves like [since](#since): it pulls a perfect tense into the main clause, takes a simple past in its own clause, and adds a quiet insistence that the stretch has run unbroken. Because the same two words are also an adverb and a preposition, the clause test still decides: a subject and a verb after it make it a conjunction, a noun alone makes it a preposition, and nothing at all makes it an adverb.
examples: Ever since the plant closed, the diner has been half empty.
He's been afraid of dogs ever since one bit him in third grade.
Ever since she started running, she's slept better.
The back porch has leaked ever since we bought the place.
Ever since they added the third shift, the parking lot has been a mess.
We had one argument about it in 2019, and he's brought it up ever since. (bare adverb - no clause follows)
She's kept the same phone number ever since college. (preposition - a noun phrase, not a clause)

entries.clause: adverbial clause of time
entries.pattern: From the time [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] from the time [clause]. · From the time [clause] until [clause], [main clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the from the time clause when it comes first; no comma when it follows. In the from ... until pairing, no comma between the two halves.
entries.meaning: The unambiguous way to say what since says: it marks the start of a stretch, with no chance of being misread as 'because.' It also does not force a perfect tense on the main clause, so it can frame a stretch that ended long ago - from the time he was six, he played piano every day.
examples: From the time she was six, she played piano every single day.
He was suspicious from the time they walked in.
From the moment the doors opened, the line never got shorter.
From the time the alarm sounded until the last truck pulled out, it was nine minutes.
We knew from the time the offer came in that it wasn't serious.
From the day he retired, he never set an alarm again.

entries.register: neutral in the uninverted order (We had hardly sat down when...); formal to literary when hardly is fronted and the subject inverts
entries.clause: adverbial clause of time (when here is locked to the correlative and cannot be traded for than; on its own the same word heads noun clauses and relative clauses too - see [when](#when))
entries.pattern: Hardly had [subject] [past participle] when [clause]. · Scarcely / Barely had [subject] [past participle] when [clause]. · [Subject] had hardly [past participle] when [clause]. · Hardly had [subject] [past participle] before [clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma before when, and no comma inside the inverted opening. Fronting hardly forces subject-auxiliary inversion: Hardly had she left when..., never Hardly she had left when...
entries.meaning: Says the second event followed the first almost instantly, framed from the angle that the first had barely finished. Pair hardly, scarcely, and barely with when (or before); pair no sooner with than. Crossing the pairs - no sooner ... when, hardly ... than - is the classic error with both patterns.
examples: Hardly had she left when the phone rang.
We had hardly sat down when the fire alarm went off.
Scarcely had the ink dried when the whole deal fell apart.
Barely had the plane leveled off when the seatbelt sign came back on.
Hardly had the words left my mouth when I regretted them.
The rain had scarcely stopped when the kids were back outside.

entries.clause: adverbial clause of time
entries.pattern: Next time [clause], [main clause]. · The next time [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] next time [clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the next time clause when it comes first; no comma when it follows.
entries.meaning: Points at the first occasion still to come. The bare form (next time you're in town) is the conversational default; the next time is a little more formal and is preferred when the occasion is a specific one already under discussion.
examples: Next time you're in town, call me.
I'll bring the good camera next time we go.
The next time somebody asks, tell them to email me.
Next time the alarm goes off at three in the morning, I'm unplugging it.
Ask for Dana next time you call.
The next time she came through Denver, we finally met for coffee.

entries.respell: noh-SOO-ner … THAN, than reducing to thun
entries.clause: adverbial clause of time (than here is the correlative partner of no sooner, not the comparative conjunction of taller than I am and not the preposition of older than me)
entries.pattern: No sooner had [subject] [past participle] than [clause]. · No sooner [did / was / were] [subject] [verb] than [clause]. · [Subject] had no sooner [past participle] than [clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma before than. Fronting no sooner forces subject-auxiliary inversion: No sooner had we sat down than..., never No sooner we had sat down than... When the clause has no auxiliary of its own, do supplies one: No sooner did I sit down than...
variants: no sooner … but (archaic and now nonstandard)
than here is the correlative partner word, not the comparative conjunction of bigger than I thought
entries.meaning: The most emphatic way in English to say that one event followed another instantly. The partner word is than, never when - No sooner had she left when the phone rang is the single most common mistake made with this pattern, and hardly, scarcely, and barely are the words that take when.
examples: No sooner had we sat down than the waiter took our order.
No sooner had the game started than the power went out.
She had no sooner hung up than the phone rang again.
No sooner did I get comfortable than somebody knocked on the door.
No sooner was the paint dry than the kids put handprints on it.
He had no sooner unpacked than the company transferred him again.

entries.ipa: /nɑt ənˈtɪl/; in the ordinary order the negative contracts: didn't ... until /ˈdɪdənt/
entries.register: neutral in the ordinary order; formal to emphatic when fronted
entries.clause: adverbial clause of time, negated
entries.pattern: [negative main clause] until [clause] (the ordinary order: He didn't call until Tuesday). · Not until [clause] [auxiliary] [subject] [verb] (fronted, with inversion). · Not until [noun phrase] [auxiliary] [subject] [verb]. · It was not until [clause or noun phrase] that [clause] (the cleft, which needs no inversion).
entries.punctuation: No comma before until in the ordinary order, and - this is the exception worth memorizing - no comma after the fronted not until clause either. It is the one fronted time clause in this file that takes no comma, because the inversion already marks the break. Fronting forces subject-auxiliary inversion: Not until the results came back did anyone relax, never Not until the results came back anyone relaxed. When the clause has no auxiliary of its own, do supplies one.
variants: it was not until … that (the cleft)
entries.meaning: English's way of saying 'at that point and no earlier.' The plain order is unremarkable - The store doesn't open until ten - but fronting not until turns the sentence into one of the negative-inversion patterns, alongside no sooner ... than and hardly ... when, and it is what journalists and speechwriters reach for when they want the length of the delay to land. The it was not until ... that cleft says the same thing without the inversion and is much easier to get right.
examples: Not until the last box was on the truck did anybody sit down.
He didn't say a word about the diagnosis until the semester was over. (ordinary order - no inversion)
Not until 1974 did the state require seat belts in school buses.
It was not until she read the second page that she understood what he was actually asking. (cleft)
Not until the power came back on did we realize how cold the house had gotten.
Not until you have done it yourself will you understand why it takes three days.

entries.clause: adverbial clause of time and cause
entries.pattern: Now that [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] now that [clause]. · Now [clause], [main clause] (informal, with that dropped).
entries.punctuation: Comma after the now that clause when it comes first; no comma when it follows.
entries.meaning: Fuses time and cause: it means 'from this point on, and because of it.' Since and because give a reason with no time anchor, while now that insists that the situation has just changed. The clause almost always takes the present or the present perfect.
examples: Now that the semester's over, I can finally sleep in.
He's much easier to work with now that he's not commuting.
Now that you mention it, I did hear something about that.
Now that the kids are both in school, the house is unnervingly quiet.
We can afford it now that the car is paid off.
Now that she's seen the actual numbers, she's asking better questions.

entries.register: neutral in the trailing order; formal to emphatic when fronted
entries.clause: adverbial clause of time, focused
entries.pattern: [main clause] only when [clause] (the ordinary order). · Only when [clause] [auxiliary] [subject] [verb] (fronted, with inversion). · Only after [clause or noun phrase] [auxiliary] [subject] [verb]. · Only once [clause] [auxiliary] [subject] [verb]. · It is only when [clause] that [clause] (the cleft).
entries.punctuation: No comma in the trailing order, and no comma after the fronted clause either - like not until, the inversion marks the break, so Only when the rain stopped did they start takes none. Fronting forces subject-auxiliary inversion: Only after she left did he speak, never Only after she left he spoke; when there is no auxiliary, do supplies one.
variants: it is only when … that (the cleft)
entries.meaning: Only clamped onto a time clause narrows the main clause down to that one occasion and rules out every other: he relaxes only when the shift ends says there is no other moment. Swap the subordinator to move the point - only when names the moment, only after puts the main clause behind it, only once adds the sense of a threshold finally crossed - and the construction stays the same in all three. Fronted, it behaves exactly like [not until](#not-until) and inverts, and that inverted form is both the emphatic one and the one learners most often get wrong.
examples: Only when the last guest had gone did she admit how tired she was.
The heat kicks on only when the temperature drops below sixty.
Only after the audit was finished did the board see the actual numbers.
Only once the paperwork clears will the money move.
He talks about his father only when somebody else brings him up first.
Only when you have taught it yourself do you understand how hard it is.

entries.type: subordinating (connective relative) in the linking use; interrogative adverb in the challenge use
entries.register: formal and British-leaning as a connective; sharply informal in the rhetorical question
entries.clause: adverbial relative clause of time, always non-restrictive, with when pointing back at a date or event already named. The question use builds no clause at all and connects nothing.
entries.pattern: [main clause naming a point in time], since when [clause with a perfect tense]. · Since when [auxiliary] [subject] [verb]? (the rhetorical question - a separate construction). · No fronted linking skeleton: the connective clause cannot open a sentence.
entries.punctuation: As a connective it is always preceded by a comma and never followed by one, and it cannot start a sentence. As a question it opens the sentence and takes a question mark: Since when do you drink coffee?
entries.meaning: Two different words wearing one spelling. The connective use ties a clause to a date already given - the mill closed in 1998, since when the town has lost a third of its population - and it is formal, faintly British, and uncommon in American prose, where and since then does the job. The other use is a challenge rather than a connector: Since when is that my job? expects no answer and means 'that was never true.' Only the first belongs in a grammar of conjunctions, but the second is far more likely to reach an American ear.
examples: The mill closed in 1998, since when the town has lost a third of its population.
She was appointed to the bench in 2014, since when she has written more dissents than opinions.
The rule was suspended during the pandemic, since when nobody has bothered to reinstate it.
He gave up coffee in March, since when he has been impossible to talk to before ten.
Since when do you know anything about carburetors? (rhetorical question - not a connector)
Ordinary American English: The mill closed in 1998, and since then the town has lost a third of its population.

entries.clause: adverbial clause of time
entries.pattern: The day [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] the day [clause]. · The [time noun] [clause], [main clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the the day clause when that clause comes first; no comma when it follows. The optional that is almost always dropped.
entries.meaning: The pattern behind the moment and the minute, opened up to any unit of time: the plus a time noun plus a bare clause makes a time conjunction. Longer units give a period rather than a point, so the year we moved frames a stretch the way while does, while the day we moved names a single occasion.
examples: The day the factory closed, half the town started looking for work.
I knew the day I met him that he'd never leave Ohio.
The year we lived in Boston, it snowed into April.
The night the storm came through, we lost three trees.
She quit the week her contract ran out.
The summer I turned twelve, I read every book in the house.

entries.clause: adverbial clause of time
entries.pattern: The first time [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] the first time [clause]. · The [ordinal] time [clause], [main clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the the first time clause when that clause comes first; no comma when it follows.
entries.meaning: Singles out one occasion in a series and locates the main clause there. Because any ordinal works, the frame is a workhorse of narrative: the first time sets up a pattern that a later occasion breaks.
examples: The first time I drove in Boston, I got honked at within a block.
She said no the first time he asked.
The first time the alarm went off, everybody filed out politely.
The third time the check bounced, the landlord called a lawyer.
I stopped worrying about it the first time somebody told me it was normal.
The first time you make it, follow the recipe exactly.

entries.clause: adverbial clause of time
entries.pattern: The instant [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] the instant [clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the the instant clause when that clause comes first; no comma when it follows.
entries.meaning: The most emphatic and the most bookish member of the moment / minute / second / instant set. All four mean 'as soon as'; this one insists on a vanishing interval and shows up far more in written narrative than in speech.
examples: The instant the doors opened, the crowd surged forward.
He knew the instant he saw the number on the screen.
The instant she stepped outside, the wind took her umbrella.
The alarm trips the instant the current drops.
The instant the verdict came in, the room went silent.
She recognized the handwriting the instant she opened the envelope.

entries.clause: adverbial clause of time
entries.pattern: The last time [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] the last time [clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the the last time clause when that clause comes first; no comma when it follows.
entries.meaning: Points at the most recent occasion, or at the final one. The ambiguity between those two readings is real and usually harmless: the last time we spoke normally means 'most recently,' but in the right context it means 'for good.'
examples: The last time I saw him, he still had the beard.
The car made that same noise the last time we drove to Chicago.
The last time we tried this, the server crashed.
The last time the pipes froze, it cost us four hundred dollars.
The last time she came through town, we missed each other by a day.
The last time you asked, I gave you the same answer.

entries.clause: adverbial clause of time
entries.pattern: The minute [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] the minute [clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the the minute clause when that clause comes first; no comma when it follows.
entries.meaning: 'As soon as,' with a conversational edge. Of the four members of this set, the minute and the second are the spoken ones, the moment is the neutral one, and the instant is the literary one; the grammar is identical across all four.
examples: The minute he walked in, everybody stopped talking.
Call me the minute you hear anything.
The minute that bell rings, the hallway is a stampede.
She knew something was wrong the minute she saw his face.
The minute I sat down, the baby woke up.
We'll head out the minute the rain lets up.

entries.clause: adverbial clause of time
entries.pattern: The moment [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] the moment [clause]. · From the moment [clause], [main clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the the moment clause when that clause comes first; no comma when it follows. The optional that is normally dropped.
entries.meaning: The neutral and most usable member of the moment / minute / second / instant family: it means 'as soon as,' with more force than when and none of the bookishness of the instant. Adding from converts it from a point into a starting line.
examples: The moment the doors opened, people started pushing.
I knew the moment I walked in that I was underdressed.
The moment she started singing, the room went quiet.
Text me the moment you land.
From the moment he took the job, he was looking for the next one.
The dog hears the leash the moment you touch it.

entries.clause: adverbial clause of time
entries.pattern: The second [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] the second [clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the the second clause when that clause comes first; no comma when it follows.
entries.meaning: The most colloquial and most impatient of the four: it means 'as soon as,' and it usually carries a note of exasperation or surprise. Watch the collision with the ordinal - the second time means the second occasion, while the second on its own means 'instantly.'
examples: The second the whistle blew, both benches cleared.
He starts complaining the second the check comes.
The second I turned my back, the dog was up on the counter.
Let me know the second you hear from her.
The second the movie ended, my phone lit up.
She was out the door the second her shift ended.

entries.clause: adverbial clause of time
entries.pattern: The whole time [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] the whole time [clause]. · [main clause] the whole time (bare - an adverb, not a conjunction).
entries.punctuation: Comma after the the whole time clause when that clause comes first; no comma when it follows. The optional that is normally dropped.
entries.meaning: The duration member of the the + time-noun family: where the moment and the second name a point, this one covers every bit of a stretch. While says two things overlapped; the whole time insists the overlap was total, which is why it so often carries an accusation (he knew the whole time). It doubles as a bare adverb, and that is the test - in He knew the whole time there is no following clause, so there is no conjunction.
examples: The whole time we were talking, he was checking his phone.
She knew about the layoffs the whole time we were planning the retreat.
The whole time the inspector was in the basement, nobody said a word.
The dog sat by the front door the entire time we were gone.
The whole time I lived in Chicago, I never made it to a Cubs game.
He was standing right behind me the whole time. (bare adverb - no clause follows)

entries.ipa: /ənˈtɪl sʌtʃ ˈtaɪm əz/; the final as rarely carries stress
entries.clause: adverbial clause of time
entries.pattern: Until such time as [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] until such time as [clause]. · [main clause] until such time as [clause] and no longer.
entries.punctuation: Comma after the until such time as clause when it comes first; no comma when it follows.
variants: until such time that (a common miswriting)
entries.meaning: A four-word way to say until, at home in contracts, court orders, and policy manuals and almost nowhere else. In ordinary prose it is padding, and editors cut it back to until. It survives in legal drafting because that register wants an endpoint stated as an event whose date is unknown.
examples: The account remains frozen until such time as the court rules otherwise.
Until such time as a permanent director is appointed, Ms. Reyes will serve in an acting capacity.
Benefits continue until such time as the employee secures comparable coverage.
Until such time as the tenant cures the default, the landlord may withhold consent.
The materials shall be held in escrow until such time as both parties have signed.
Until such time as the board votes, the current policy stands.

entries.clause: adverbial clause of time and sequence, always non-restrictive
entries.pattern: [main clause], whereafter [clause]. · [long main clause]; whereafter [clause]. · There is no fronted skeleton - Whereafter [clause], [main clause] is not a sentence.
entries.punctuation: Always preceded by a comma, or by a semicolon in a long sentence; never followed by one. Like whereupon, it can never open a sentence.
variants: whereupon (the same construction with a sense of immediate consequence)
thereafter (an adverb, not a connector of clauses)
entries.meaning: The where- compound for 'after which,' and the rarest member of the family in American English: [whereupon](#whereupon) still lives in literary narrative and after which covers everything else, which leaves whereafter to contracts, arbitration clauses, and engineering specifications. It is markedly commoner in legal English written in Dutch- and Afrikaans-influenced traditions than in anything drafted in the United States. Use after which unless a house style specifically wants the where- form.
examples: The parties shall confer in good faith for thirty days, whereafter either may demand arbitration.
The notice was served on the seventeenth, whereafter the period for objection began to run.
The specimen is heated to four hundred degrees, whereafter it is quenched in oil.
The chair declared the motion carried, whereafter the meeting was adjourned.
The tenant shall vacate the premises by noon, whereafter any property left behind is deemed abandoned.
Ordinary English: The parties confer for thirty days, after which either one can demand arbitration.

entries.clause: adverbial clause of time and consequence, always non-restrictive
entries.pattern: [main clause], whereupon [clause]. · [long main clause]; whereupon [clause]. · [main clause], whereupon [clause], [continuation]. · There is no fronted skeleton - Whereupon [clause], [main clause] is ungrammatical.
entries.punctuation: Always preceded by a comma, or by a semicolon in a long sentence; never followed by one. Unlike every other subordinator in this file, its clause cannot move to the front of the sentence.
entries.meaning: Means 'and immediately after that,' with a hint that the second event was triggered by the first. Because it can only follow its main clause, it works as a narrative connector rather than a scene-setter - which is the opposite of when and after. At which point says the same thing in plain modern English.
examples: The witness refused to answer, whereupon the judge cleared the courtroom.
He announced that he was resigning, whereupon the room erupted.
The motion failed by one vote, whereupon the chair called a recess.
She read the letter twice, whereupon she folded it and put it in her pocket.
The alarm sounded, whereupon every door in the building locked automatically.
We waited an hour, at which point somebody finally told us the flight was canceled.

entries.respell: uh-GENST, also uh-GAYNST; in verse GENST
entries.register: archaic; still heard from older speakers in Appalachian and Ozark English
entries.clause: adverbial clause of time (the same word is overwhelmingly a preposition today - against the wall, against the rules - and only the clause use is the conjunction)
entries.pattern: [main clause] against [clause]. · Against [clause], [main clause]. · [imperative] against [clause] (the commonest shape: have it ready against he comes).
entries.punctuation: Comma after the against clause when it comes first; no comma when it follows. The clause takes the present or the present subjunctive even for future reference - against he come, against the weather turns - and that bare subjunctive is one of the marks of the old form.
variants: agin (eye-dialect spelling of the regional pronunciation)
in time for (when the sense is preparation)
entries.meaning: The old conjunction meaning 'by the time that,' with an extra sense of getting ready in advance for the moment named: bake the bread against they come home is about preparation, not merely sequence. An American meets it in the King James Bible, in Shakespeare and his contemporaries, and in nineteenth-century fiction that reproduces country speech, and it is still occasionally audible from older speakers in the southern mountains. Do not write it: by the time carries the timing, in time for carries the preparation, and modern readers will simply see the preposition and stall.
examples: They made the guest room ready against her father came up from Richmond.
Have the horses watered against the wagons roll at first light.
She had put up four quarts of preserves against the winter came on.
Against the parson arrives, somebody had better sweep the porch.
Lay in the wood now, against the weather turns.
Modern equivalent: They had the guest room ready by the time her father came up from Richmond.

entries.register: regional (British and Irish); not current American usage
entries.clause: adverbial clause of time (the same word is an ordinary adverb in both varieties - go directly home - and only the conjunction is foreign to American English)
entries.pattern: Directly [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] directly [clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the directly clause when it comes first; no comma when it follows.
entries.meaning: British English uses directly as a conjunction meaning 'as soon as.' American English does not: to an American ear the sentence sounds unfinished, as though directly were still an adverb. The adverb is alive and well in the United States - 'straight' (go directly home), 'immediately' (I'll deal with it directly), and in Southern speech 'in a little while' (I'll be there directly) - but only the conjunction is foreign.
examples: Directly he arrived, the meeting started. (British)
She recognized him directly he spoke. (British)
Directly the rain stopped, they were back on the field. (British)
I'll write directly I hear from the solicitor. (British)
Directly the door closed, the room went quiet. (British)
American equivalent: As soon as he arrived, the meeting started.

entries.clause: adverbial clause of time
entries.pattern: Ere [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] ere [clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the ere clause when it comes first; no comma when it follows.
entries.meaning: The archaic word for before. It survives in hymns, poetry, Shakespeare, and deliberate period style; in ordinary modern prose it reads as a joke or an affectation. Do not confuse it with e'er, which is a contraction of ever, or with err /ɜr/, which is a verb.
examples: Ere the sun sets, we must reach the pass.
He was gone ere the household stirred.
Ere the last note faded, the audience was on its feet.
She vowed to finish the letter ere the ship sailed.
Ere another winter comes, the roof will have to be replaced.
Modern equivalent: Before the sun sets, we have to reach the pass.

entries.clause: adverbial clause of time (the same word is an ordinary adverb in both varieties - call me immediately - and only the conjunction is foreign to American English)
entries.pattern: Immediately [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] immediately [clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the immediately clause when it comes first; no comma when it follows.
variants: immediately after (fully standard in American English)
entries.meaning: British English lets immediately introduce a clause on its own: Immediately the results came in, she called. American English does not - Americans hear the adverb and wait for the sentence to continue - and writes as soon as or immediately after instead. The plain adverb immediately is of course standard in both varieties.
examples: Immediately the results came in, she called her supervisor. (British)
He knew immediately the door opened that something was wrong. (British)
Immediately the ceremony ended, the caterers moved in. (British)
Immediately the engine cut out, the cabin went silent. (British)
The porter locked the gates immediately the last guest had gone. (British)
American equivalent: As soon as the results came in, she called her supervisor.
Also standard in American English: Immediately after the results came in, she called her supervisor.

entries.clause: adverbial clause of time
entries.pattern: Or ever [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] or ever [clause]. · Or ever [clause with a present subjunctive verb].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the or ever clause when it comes first; no comma when it follows. The clause frequently takes the present subjunctive in the texts where the phrase actually appears: or ever the silver cord be loosed.
variants: or e'er (the poetic spelling, easily confused with ere)
entries.meaning: An emphatic archaic before, meaning 'before ever' or 'before so much as.' The or has nothing to do with the coordinating conjunction - it is a separate old word that already meant 'before,' and the ever piles emphasis on top of it. An American meets the phrase in the King James Bible, in Hamlet, and in hymn texts, and nowhere else; it is not available for modern writing, and even deliberate period pastiche usually reaches for [ere](#ere) instead.
examples: Or ever the silver cord be loosed, remember thy Creator.
He was taken from us or ever he had reached his fortieth year.
Or ever the sun was risen, the whole household was astir.
Would I had died or ever I saw that letter.
They were seized or ever they came at the bottom of the stair.
Modern equivalent: He was taken from us before he ever reached forty.

entries.ipa: /soʊ ˈsun æz/; the final as reduces to /əz/
entries.respell: soh-SOON-az; final as reducing to uhz
entries.register: archaic; standard English into the early nineteenth century, obsolete since
entries.clause: adverbial clause of time
entries.pattern: So soon as [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] so soon as [clause]. · So soon as ever [clause], [main clause] (emphatic).
entries.punctuation: Comma after the so soon as clause when it comes first; no comma when it follows - the same rules its modern replacement takes.
variants: so long as (the one member of the so series that survived)
entries.meaning: The older form of [as soon as](#as-soon-as), ordinary in the King James Bible, in Shakespeare, and in eighteenth- and nineteenth-century prose, and gone from American English by about the time of the Civil War. The paired history is the interesting part: English kept so long as alongside as long as and still uses both, but let so soon as go completely, so a modern reader hears the phrase as a period marker rather than as a live variant. Write as soon as.
examples: So soon as the letter was sealed, he sent it away by the evening post.
She resolved to speak with him so soon as the company should withdraw.
So soon as the gates were opened, the crowd pressed in.
He begged that word be sent him so soon as the child was born.
So soon as ever the ship was sighted, the whole town went down to the quay.
Modern equivalent: As soon as the letter was sealed, he sent it out with the evening mail.

entries.register: archaic and poetic; the bare adverb survives in all the while
entries.clause: adverbial clause of time (duration). The same two words are far commoner as a bare adverb meaning 'meanwhile,' which builds no clause at all.
entries.pattern: [main clause] the while [clause]. · The while [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] the while (bare adverb - nothing follows). · All the while [clause], [main clause] (the surviving modern form).
entries.punctuation: Comma after the the while clause when it comes first; no comma when it follows. No commas at all around the bare adverb at the end of a clause: he watched her, smiling the while.
entries.meaning: The archaic conjunction while with the definite article welded on, at home in verse, hymn texts, and nineteenth-century narrative: she sang, the while the fire burned low. Modern English kept only two pieces of it - the bare adverb (smiling the while) and the intensified conjunction all the while, which is ordinary today - and left the plain conjunction behind. Read it as a period marker and write while or all the while.
examples: He kept his eyes on the road, the while she read the letter aloud.
The while the choir sang, the candles were carried down the aisle.
She sat with her hands folded, praying the while. (bare adverb - no clause follows)
The old man mended his nets, the while his grandson counted gulls.
The while the storm held, not a soul stirred from the inn.
Current English: He kept his eyes on the road all the while she read the letter aloud.

entries.ipa: /wɑt ˈtaɪm/, also /wʌt ˈtaɪm/; /ʍɑt/ for speakers who keep the wh
entries.respell: wot-TIME, also wut-TIME; HWOT for speakers who keep the wh
entries.clause: adverbial clause of time (the same two words open an ordinary question - What time does it start? - which is a different construction entirely)
entries.pattern: What time [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] what time [clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the what time clause when it comes first; no comma when it follows.
variants: the interrogative what time (What time is the train?), a separate construction
entries.meaning: The archaic conjunction meaning 'at the time when.' It is preserved for most American readers in a single line of the King James Psalms - What time I am afraid, I will trust in thee - and it turns up elsewhere in Milton, in hymnody, and in nineteenth-century verse. Nothing in modern prose licenses it, and the collision with the everyday question is fatal: a reader who meets what time the reapers went out hears a question about the clock and has to back up. Write when.
examples: What time I am afraid, I will trust in thee.
What time the morning star arose, the watch was set upon the wall.
He came to her what time the household slept.
What time the reapers went into the field, the sky was still dark.
The bells were rung what time the news reached the village.
Modern equivalent: When I am afraid, I trust in you.

entries.respell: wen-THAT; that usually reducing to thut
entries.register: archaic; standard in Middle and early Modern English
entries.clause: adverbial clause of time
entries.pattern: When that [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] when that [clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the when that clause when it comes first; no comma when it follows.
variants: before that (the same old that-tagging on other subordinators)
entries.meaning: Plain when with the old subordinating particle that still attached. Middle and early Modern English tagged that onto most subordinators - when that, if that, though that - and the language shed the particle across the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, keeping it only where it had fused into a new word (now that, so that, in that). Modern readers meet it at the head of the Canterbury Tales and in Feste's closing song in Twelfth Night. Do not reproduce it outside period pastiche.
examples: When that I was and a little tiny boy, the rain it raineth every day.
When that April with his showers sweet had pierced the drought of March, then folk longed to go on pilgrimage.
He shall be sorely missed when that the summer comes.
When that the trumpet sounds, the dead shall be raised incorruptible.
She wept when that the letter was read out to the household.
Modern equivalent: When I was a little boy, the rain it raineth every day.

entries.clause: adverbial clause of time; in some older texts adverbial of contrast instead, where it means 'whereas'
entries.pattern: Whenas [clause], [main clause]. · Whenas [clause], then [main clause] (the correlative shape common in verse). · [main clause] whenas [clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the whenas clause when it comes first; no comma when it follows.
variants: when as (two words, the older spelling)
whereas (the surviving relative of the contrast sense)
when (the modern form of the time sense)
entries.meaning: An Elizabethan and Jacobean conjunction meaning 'when' or 'at the time when,' and occasionally 'whereas.' The line most Americans have met it in is Herrick's - Whenas in silks my Julia goes - and outside seventeenth-century verse it is genuinely dead, not merely formal or literary but obsolete. Note how the family split: the contrast sense survived as whereas, which is standard today in contracts and in ordinary argument, while the time sense left the language altogether.
examples: Whenas in silks my Julia goes, then, then methinks how sweetly flows that liquefaction of her clothes.
Whenas the day was far spent, they came unto the city.
He was ever the first to speak, whenas the others held their peace.
Whenas the frost is on the ground, the roads are hard and quick.
Whenas she looked upon him, her colour rose.
Modern equivalent: When my Julia walks by in silks, I think how sweetly her clothes flow.

entries.ipa: /waɪlz/; also /ʍaɪlz/ for speakers who keep the wh
entries.register: archaic; the separate adverb whiles meaning 'sometimes' survives in Scots and Northern English
entries.clause: adverbial clause of time (duration)
entries.pattern: Whiles [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] whiles [clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the whiles clause when it comes first; no comma when it follows.
variants: the while (the same word with different old endings)
whiles meaning 'sometimes' (a separate adverbial use, current in Scots)
entries.meaning: The old -s form of while, ordinary in the King James Bible - agree with thine adversary quickly, whiles thou art in the way with him - and out of English prose by the eighteenth century. It sits at one end of a set of four: while is the American standard, whilst is current British, and whiles and the while are archaic. Recognize it in reading and leave it in the seventeenth century.
examples: Agree with thine adversary quickly, whiles thou art in the way with him.
Whiles the bridegroom tarried, they all slumbered and slept.
He kept the watch whiles the others rested.
Whiles I live, thou shalt want for nothing.
The bread was eaten whiles it was yet warm.
Modern equivalent: Settle with your accuser quickly, while you are still on the way to court with him.

entries.register: British; in American English an affectation
entries.clause: adverbial clause of time (also contrast)
entries.pattern: Whilst [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] whilst [clause]. · whilst + [-ing form].
entries.punctuation: The same rules as while: comma after the whilst clause when it comes first; no comma when it follows in the time sense, and a comma when it means 'whereas.'
entries.meaning: Identical in meaning to while and about as common as while in British writing. In American English it is rare, and when it does appear it reads as either British or self-consciously fancy; American style guides recommend while in every case. It is in this file so that learners recognize it and know not to reach for it.
examples: Whilst the committee deliberated, the applicants waited outside. (British)
She read the report whilst the kettle boiled. (British)
Whilst in London, he kept a diary. (British)
The system remains offline whilst maintenance is carried out. (British)
Whilst I take your point, the deadline hasn't moved. (British; contrast sense)
American equivalent: While the committee deliberated, the applicants waited outside.

entries.clause: none - it modifies a clause; the clause it sits in stays independent
entries.pattern: [independent clause]; afterward, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. Afterward, [independent clause]. · [subject] [verb] afterward.
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it when it links two independent clauses - We ate, afterward we walked is a comma splice. Comma after it when it opens a clause; no commas at all when it sits at the end (We walked afterward).
entries.meaning: The adverb counterpart of the conjunction after: it points back at something already mentioned instead of naming it again. Because it is an adverb it can slide around inside its clause, which is exactly the test that separates it from a real conjunction.
examples: The ceremony ran long; afterward, nobody wanted to stand around for photos.
We toured the plant. Afterward, they fed us in the cafeteria.
She apologized afterward, which surprised everybody.
He said almost nothing during the meeting and even less afterward.
Take the pill with food; afterward, drink a full glass of water.
They stayed friends for a while afterward, then drifted apart.

entries.clause: none - an adverbial phrase; its clause remains independent
entries.pattern: At first, [independent clause]; [later / then / eventually], [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. At first, [independent clause]. · [subject] [verb phrase] at first, but [independent clause]. · [subject] [verb phrase] at first.
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it when it links two independent clauses - At first he said no, later he changed his mind is a comma splice. A comma works only with a coordinating conjunction: At first he said no, but later he changed his mind. Comma after it when it opens a clause, though a phrase this short is often left bare (At first nobody said anything), and both are standard. No comma when it sits at the end.
variants: at first glance / at first blush (different phrases - they concede an appearance rather than mark a time)
entries.meaning: The opener of a two-part timeline: it plants a first state that something later overturns, which is why it almost always arrives with a partner - later, then, eventually, but. Left without one it strands the reader, because At first, the engine ran fine is a promise that the engine stopped running fine. Initially is the report-writing equivalent and carries the same promise; plain first is a list marker and carries none.
examples: At first, nobody believed the number; then accounting ran it again.
She hated the job at first, but the people won her over.
At first the engine ran fine. By the second lap it was smoking.
The pay looked good at first.
At first, we thought the noise was the furnace; eventually we found the raccoon.
He wasn't going to say anything at first, and then he couldn't help himself.

entries.ipa: /æt ðə ˈseɪm ˌtaɪm/, at reducing to /ət/
entries.clause: none - an adverbial phrase; its clause remains independent. The variant at the same time that is a true subordinator and does take a clause.
entries.pattern: [independent clause]; at the same time, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. At the same time, [independent clause]. · [subject] [verb] and, at the same time, [verb] ... · At the same time that [clause], [main clause] (the subordinating variant).
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it when it links two independent clauses - It's expensive, at the same time nothing else works is a comma splice. Comma after it when it opens a clause, and commas on both sides mid-clause. The subordinating at the same time that takes the ordinary subordinator rules instead: comma after the clause when it comes first, none when it follows.
variants: all the same (concessive only - a different phrase)
entries.meaning: Does two jobs, and the second one has quietly taken over. Literally it means 'simultaneously,' the way meanwhile does. In practice it far more often means 'and yet,' conceding a point while holding the line: It's expensive; at the same time, nothing else does the job. Read the whole sentence before deciding which is meant, because the concessive use has no time content at all.
examples: The store was hiring; at the same time, corporate was closing two locations.
She wanted the promotion. At the same time, she dreaded the travel. (concessive)
He's the best writer on staff and, at the same time, the hardest to edit.
At the same time that the city was cutting bus routes, it was breaking ground on a streetcar. (subordinating variant)
The proposal saves money; at the same time, it costs us a year.
At the same time, nobody wants to be the one who says no.

entries.clause: none - an adverb; its clause remains independent
entries.pattern: [independent clause]; eventually, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. Eventually, [independent clause]. · [subject] eventually [verb] ... · [subject] [verb phrase] eventually.
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it when it links two independent clauses - We waited, eventually somebody came is a comma splice. Comma after it when it opens a clause; no commas at all when it sits inside the clause (She eventually agreed) or at the end (He'll come around eventually).
entries.meaning: Puts the second event at the far end of an unspecified delay: 'after a while, and it took a while.' Then is neutral about the gap and afterward only says 'later'; eventually is the one that reports the waiting. It is also a standing trap for learners of Romance languages - Spanish eventualmente and French éventuellement mean 'possibly,' not 'at last.'
examples: The line barely moved; eventually, they opened a second register.
We called four different plumbers. Eventually, one of them showed up.
She eventually stopped asking about it.
Eventually, somebody is going to have to tell him.
The paperwork sat on his desk for a month; eventually, HR called him about it.
He'll come around eventually.

entries.ipa: /ˈfaɪnəli/, commonly compressed to /ˈfaɪnli/ in fast speech
entries.clause: none - an adverb; its clause remains independent
entries.pattern: [independent clause]; finally, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. Finally, [independent clause]. · [subject] finally [verb] ... · First ..., then ..., finally ... · [subject] [verb phrase] finally.
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it when it links two independent clauses - We waited two hours, finally somebody came out is a comma splice. Comma after it when it opens a clause; no commas when it sits inside the clause (She finally answered) or at the end. In a list of steps it takes the comma the last item would take anyway: ..., and finally add the zest.
entries.meaning: Does two jobs, and a reader has to tell them apart. In a sequence it simply marks the last item - first ... then ... finally - and carries no feeling at all. In a narrative it means 'at last, after too long a wait,' and carries relief or irritation: The line finally moved. [Eventually](#eventually) reports the delay flatly; finally reports how the delay felt. Lastly only ever does the list job, which is why The line lastly moved is impossible.
examples: We waited two hours; finally, somebody came out to explain.
Whisk the eggs, fold in the flour, and finally add the zest.
She finally answered on the fourth try.
Finally, I'd like to thank the volunteers who set up the room.
The permit sat in review all spring. Finally, in July, it cleared.
He said he'd call back, and after three days he finally did.

entries.clause: none - an adverb; its clause remains independent
entries.pattern: [independent clause]; henceforth, [independent clause]. · Henceforth, [independent clause]. · [subject] shall henceforth [verb].
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it when it links two independent clauses; comma after it when it opens one. No comma when it sits inside a verb phrase: shall henceforth be known as.
entries.meaning: Marks a boundary after which a new rule applies: 'starting now and continuing.' It belongs to statutes, bylaws, and proclamations; in ordinary prose from now on does the same work without the costume. Thereafter is its past-reference twin.
