examples: The building shall henceforth be known as the Hall of Sciences.
The old form is discontinued; henceforth, all requests go through the portal.
Henceforth, no employee may approve their own expenses.
The rate is fixed for two years; henceforth, it floats with the index.
The committee will henceforth meet quarterly rather than monthly. (mid-clause - no commas)
I've said my piece, and henceforth I'll leave the matter to the board.

entries.clause: none - an adverbial phrase; its clause remains independent
entries.pattern: [independent clause]; in the meantime, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. In the meantime, [independent clause]. · [subject], in the meantime, [verb] ...
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it when it links two independent clauses; a comma alone is a splice. Comma after it when it opens a clause, and commas on both sides when it sits mid-clause.
entries.meaning: Fills the gap between now and an expected event: 'while we wait for that to happen.' Meanwhile simply reports that two things overlap; in the meantime almost always implies a pending outcome, which is why it so often introduces an instruction.
examples: The permit takes six weeks; in the meantime, we can order materials.
Your replacement laptop ships Monday. In the meantime, use the loaner.
In the meantime, nobody is to speak to the press.
She's still waiting on the diagnosis and, in the meantime, trying not to read anything online.
The road reopens in the spring; in the meantime, take the county highway.
In the meantime, I'd keep a copy of everything you send them.

entries.ipa: /ˈleɪtər/; the t is a flap in ordinary American speech, /ˈleɪɾər/
entries.clause: none - an adverb; its clause remains independent (the same word is also the comparative form of the adjective late, where it modifies a noun and connects nothing: a later flight)
entries.pattern: [independent clause]; later, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. Later, [independent clause]. · [subject] [verb phrase] later. · [measure phrase] later, [independent clause] (Two weeks later, the check arrived).
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it when it links two independent clauses - We ate dinner, later we walked to the pier is a comma splice. Comma after it when it opens a clause; no comma when it sits at the end (We walked to the pier later). The measure-phrase opener takes a comma after the whole phrase: Ten minutes later, the power came back.
variants: see you later (a fixed farewell, not a connector)
entries.meaning: The plainest way to put one event after another without committing to how big the gap was. [Afterward](#afterward) points specifically back at the event just named; later only says 'further along the line.' Its most useful form is the measure-phrase opener, which is how English narrative moves the clock in a single stroke: Ten minutes later, the power came back. Watch the collision with the adjective - a later flight is a modifier inside a noun phrase and joins nothing to anything.
examples: We ate dinner at the hotel; later, we walked down to the pier.
Two weeks later, the check finally arrived.
She said she'd think about it. Later, she admitted she'd already decided.
He apologized, though only much later.
The store closed in March; later on, a bakery took the space.
I'll deal with the email later.

entries.clause: none - an adverb; its clause remains independent
entries.pattern: [independent clause]; meanwhile, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. Meanwhile, [independent clause]. · [subject], meanwhile, [verb] ...
entries.punctuation: This is the rule learners get wrong most often. Meanwhile is an adverb, not a conjunction, so The kids napped, meanwhile I cleaned is a comma splice. Use a semicolon or a period before it and a comma after it; mid-clause it takes commas on both sides.
entries.meaning: The adverb that does the job of the conjunction while: it reports that a second situation was going on at the same time, without subordinating either one. Use while when you want one clause tucked inside the other; use meanwhile when both deserve to stand as sentences.
examples: The kids napped; meanwhile, I cleaned the entire kitchen.
Sales fell for the third straight quarter. Meanwhile, costs kept climbing.
He was still arguing with the gate agent. His flight, meanwhile, was boarding.
Meanwhile, back at the office, nobody had noticed he was gone.
The city debated the plan for two years; meanwhile, the building sat empty.
She trained all winter. Meanwhile, her old teammates had moved up a division.

entries.ipa: /ˈnɛkst θɪŋ ju ˈnoʊ/; you almost always reduces to /jə/ and the phrase runs together as /ˈnɛksθɪŋjəˈnoʊ/
entries.clause: none - a fixed adverbial formula; the clause it sits in front of stays independent
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]. Next thing you know, [independent clause]. · [independent clause]; next thing you know, [independent clause]. · [independent clause], and the next thing I knew, [independent clause]. · The next thing [subject] knew, [independent clause].
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it when it links two independent clauses - He borrowed the truck, next thing you know it's in Tulsa is a comma splice, common as that is in speech. Comma after it when it opens a sentence; in the run-on spoken form joined by and, the comma after it is usually left out.
variants: the next thing you knew (past narrative)
entries.meaning: The storyteller's jump cut. It marks a turn that was fast, unplanned, and slightly out of the speaker's hands, which is why it almost always introduces something absurd or unwelcome - nobody says next thing you know, everything went according to plan. The present tense keeps the story vivid even when the events are decades old, while the past form (the next thing I knew) is the one that fits written narrative. Grammatically it connects nothing: it is an adverbial formula parked in front of an independent clause, so it takes a period or a semicolon in front of it and never a bare comma.
examples: He said he'd stay for one drink. Next thing you know, he's doing karaoke.
I let the kid borrow the truck for an afternoon; next thing you know, it's registered in Tulsa.
You start with one tomato plant, and the next thing you know the whole yard is tomatoes.
The car spun once on the ice, and the next thing I knew we were facing the wrong way in the median.
She agreed to help with one bake sale. Next thing you know, she was running the PTA.
A pipe froze in January; next thing you know, we were replacing the entire kitchen floor.

entries.clause: none - an adverb; its clause remains independent
entries.pattern: [independent clause]; previously, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. Previously, [independent clause]. · [subject] had previously [past participle]. · previously [past participle] (inside a modifier: previously unreported payments).
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it when it links two independent clauses - The bridge reopened Monday, previously traffic went through Elmwood is a comma splice. Comma after it when it opens a clause. No commas when it sits inside a verb phrase (had previously testified) or in front of a participle (previously undisclosed).
variants: formerly (a former identity rather than an earlier event)
entries.meaning: The mirror of subsequently: it points back to something that happened before the moment under discussion. Reports and news writing lean on it because it keeps a timeline explicit without spending a whole before clause on it. Formerly is not a substitute - formerly the county courthouse names an old identity, while previously scheduled names an earlier event.
examples: The bridge reopened Monday; previously, traffic had been routed through Elmwood.
She previously worked for the state auditor.
The company denied the report. Previously, it had refused to comment at all.
Two of the samples had previously tested clean.
Previously, only department heads could approve overtime.
The filing lists several previously undisclosed payments.

entries.clause: none - an adverbial phrase; its clause remains independent
entries.pattern: [independent clause]; since then, [independent clause with a perfect tense]. · [Independent clause]. Since then, [independent clause]. · [subject] [has/have] [past participle] since then.
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it when it links two independent clauses - He moved out in March, since then the place has been quiet is a comma splice. Comma after it when it opens a clause; no comma when it sits at the end.
variants: ever since (as a bare adverb: He hasn't called ever since)
entries.meaning: The adverb that does what the conjunction since does, except that it points back at a moment already on the page instead of naming one: since then is since plus an anaphor. Like the conjunction it pulls a perfect tense into its clause. From then on is the forward-rolling twin and does not need the perfect.
examples: The plant closed in 2011; since then, the population has dropped by half.
She had one bad experience with a landlord. Since then, she's read every lease twice.
Nobody has heard from him since then.
Since then, the rules have changed twice.
They repaved the road in June; since then, the potholes have stayed away.
He apologized once, and from then on the subject never came up again.

entries.clause: none - an adverb; its clause remains independent
entries.pattern: [independent clause]; subsequently, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. Subsequently, [independent clause]. · [subject] was subsequently [past participle].
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it when it links two independent clauses; comma after it when it opens one. No commas when it sits inside a verb phrase: was subsequently withdrawn.
entries.meaning: The formal-register way to say 'afterward,' standard in reports, case histories, and news writing. It carries no implication of cause, which is the trap: subsequently means 'after,' consequently means 'therefore,' and swapping them changes the claim.
examples: The drug was approved in 2019 and subsequently withdrawn.
He denied the allegation; subsequently, he resigned.
Subsequently, the committee revised its own recommendation.
Two of the three witnesses subsequently changed their statements.
The property was sold at auction and subsequently demolished.
The paper was published in March. Subsequently, three labs failed to replicate it.

entries.clause: none - an adverb; its clause remains independent
entries.pattern: [independent clause]; then [independent clause]. · [independent clause], and then [independent clause]. · [subject] then [verb] ... · First ..., then ..., finally ...
entries.punctuation: Then is an adverb, not a conjunction, so a comma alone cannot hold two independent clauses together with it: We ate, then we left is a comma splice. Use a semicolon or a period, or add a coordinating conjunction - We ate; then we left, We ate. Then we left., We ate, and then we left. Unlike however and meanwhile, then normally takes no comma after it. In the if ... then pairing the comma goes before then, not after it.
entries.meaning: The workhorse sequencer of spoken English: it puts one event after another. The comma splice with then is so common in speech-like prose that it barely registers, but it is still a splice, and adding and is the painless fix. Then also has a resultative use (if that's true, then we have a problem) and a noun-modifying one (the then governor).
examples: Brown the onions; then add the garlic.
We finished unloading the boxes, and then somebody suggested pizza.
She looked at the bill, then looked at me. (no splice - one subject, two verbs)
First rinse the beans; then soak them overnight.
If the light's still red, then the sensor never reset.
He was quiet for a long moment. Then he laughed.

entries.clause: none - an adverb; its clause remains independent
entries.pattern: [independent clause]; thereafter, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. Thereafter, [independent clause]. · [time expression] thereafter.
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it when it links two independent clauses; comma after it when it opens one. No comma inside a fixed phrase like monthly thereafter or shortly thereafter.
entries.meaning: 'After that time,' pointing back at a moment already established. It is the past-reference partner of henceforth and lives in contracts, obituaries, and formal narrative, where afterward is the everyday word. The frozen phrase shortly thereafter is the form most Americans actually produce.
examples: The first payment is due on signing, and monthly thereafter.
He was elected in 1974 and served four terms thereafter.
The plant closed in March. Thereafter, the town lost a third of its population.
She left the company in 2019 and shortly thereafter started her own firm.
The lease renews automatically each year thereafter unless either party objects.
The alarm was disabled at 2:14 a.m.; thereafter, the cameras recorded nothing.
